title: The Field and the Knower
body:
The Field and the Knower

To lift Arjuna from his despair, Sree Krishna begins His discourse not with military strategy, but with supreme metaphysics. He establishes the fundamental distinction between the perishable physical body (the field, or Kshetra) and the indestructible, eternal spiritual entity that resides within (the knower of the field, or Kshetrajna). This is the basis of all Vedantic inquiry.

श्रीभगवानुवाच ।
अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे ।
गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः ।।

"The Supreme Lord said: While you speak words of wisdom, you are mourning for that which is not worthy of grief. The wise lament neither for the living nor for the dead."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 11

The Lord explains that death is merely a transition of the soul from one physical medium to another. To mourn the destruction of the body is as foolish as mourning the discarding of worn-out clothing. The soul is indestructible, unchangeable, and eternal. It is neither born nor does it ever die.

न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः ।
न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम् ।।

"Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor all these kings; nor in the future shall any of us cease to be."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 12

देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा ।
तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति ।।

"Just as the embodied soul continuously passes from childhood to youth to old age, similarly, at the time of death, the soul passes into another body. The wise are not deluded by this."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 13

In your signature Visishtadvaita-biased metaphysical style, the individual soul (jeevaathma) is understood as an eternal, infinitesimal fragment of Sriman Narayana. It is indestructible, unbreakable, and everlasting. To describe the subtle nature of the soul, your text preserves the classic Upanishadic analogy: if you take the tip of a single hair and divide it into a hundred parts, and then take one of those parts and divide it repeatedly by hundreds, that microscopic, invisible point represents the size of the soul—yet its consciousness is powerful enough to pervade and animate the entire physical body.

अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम् ।
विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित्कर्तुमर्हति ।।

"That which pervades the entire body, know it to be indestructible. No one can cause the destruction of the imperishable soul."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 17

न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः ।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ।।

"The soul is neither born nor does it ever die; nor having once existed, does it ever cease to be. The soul is without birth, eternal, immortal, and ageless. It is not destroyed when the body is destroyed."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 20

वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि ।
तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही ।।

"As a person sheds worn-out garments and wears new ones, likewise, at the time of death, the soul casts of its worn-out body and enters a new one."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 22

अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च ।
नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः ।।

"The soul is unbreakable and incombustible; it can neither be dampened nor dried. It is everlasting, in all places, unalterable, immutable, and primordial."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 24

अव्यक्तोऽयमचिन्त्योऽयमविकार्योऽयमुच्यते ।
तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि ।।

"The soul is spoken of as invisible, inconceivable, and unchangeable. Knowing this, you should not grieve for the body."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 25

देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत ।
तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि ।।

"O Arjuna, the soul that dwells within the body is immortal; therefore, you should not mourn for anyone."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 30

Sree Krishna expands this teaching by explaining the relationship between the soul, the material world, and the Supreme Lord. Under the Visishtadvaita framework, all living beings are a combination of the field (Prakriti) and the knower of the field (Jeevaathma), both of which are inseparably integrated as the body of the Supreme Soul (Paramaathma), who is their ultimate inner ruler (Antaryaami).

अन्ये त्वेवमजानन्तः श्रुत्वान्येभ्य उपासते ।
तेऽपि चातितरन्त्येव मृत्युं श्रुतिपरायणाः ।।

"There are still others who are unaware of these spiritual paths, but they hear from others and begin worshipping the Supreme Lord. By such devotion to hearing from saints, they too can gradually cross over the ocean of birth and death."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XIII, Verse 26

यावत्सञ्जायते किञ्चित्सत्वं स्थावरजङ्गमम् ।
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञसंयोगात्तद्विद्धि भरतर्षभ ।।

"O best of the Bharatas, whatever moving or unmoving being you see in existence, know it to be a combination of the field of activities and the knower of the field."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XIII, Verse 27

अनादित्वान्निर्गुणत्वात्परमात्मायमव्ययः ।
शरीरस्थोऽपि कौन्तेय न करोति न लिप्यते ।।

"The Supreme Soul is imperishable, without beginning, and devoid of any material qualities, O son of Kunti. Although situated within the body, It neither acts nor is It tainted by the material energy."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XIII, Verse 32

यथा सर्वगतं सौक्ष्म्यादाकाशं नोपलिप्यते ।
सर्वत्रावस्थितो देहे तथात्मा नोपलिप्यते ।।

"Space holds everything within it, but is subtle, and does not get contaminated by what it holds. Similarly, though its consciousness pervades the body, the soul is not affected by the attributes of the body."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XIII, Verse 33

★ THE COMPARATIVE VEDANTIC PERSPECTIVE ★
Advaita Perspective: The individual soul is essentially identical to Brahman. Individuality is an illusory projection of Avidya (ignorance) and lasts only as long as the soul identifies with the limiting adjuncts (Upadhis) of the body-mind complex. Realization dissolves this boundary, revealing absolute non-difference.
Visishtadvaita Perspective: The soul (Jeevaathma) is an eternal, real, and conscious entity that remains eternally distinct from the Lord, serving as a mode (Prakara) or attribute of the Supreme. Sree Krishna, as the Antaryaami, dwells within the soul to give it energy, yet remains completely untainted by its worldly karma (Putatman).
